findings.what: "A swapped chain of functions still gives a proper number, just a different one" is false, and the lesson's own steps 11-12 show it: input 2 gets no value from "take 4, then square root" but gives -2.59 with the root first. Say a swap can also change whether there is an answer at all. Also soften "unlike the jobs on a cable", because some cable jobs can be done in either order too.

"Textbooks add that UK books often shorten f(g(x)) to fg(x), with g still going first" has no source and reads garbled ("Textbooks add that UK books"). Cite Bitesize Higher's "fg(x) is calculated by finding g(x) first, and then substituting this into the function f" (research notes 4.7) and say it plainly.

The screen never says that the 0.5 on the join is the fraction of full pressure difference, so it is unclear what "Flow goes as the square root of that" refers to, and the reason (pressure difference goes as the square of the flow) is skipped. Yet the hints on steps 8 and 10 call the join value "the pressure difference". Suggested wording: "...so 12 mA puts 0.5, half the full pressure difference, on the join. The pressure difference goes as the square of the flow, so Q takes the square root: 0.707, 71% of full flow."

findings.where: step 9 "A root too many" (and explain, paragraph 3)
findings.what: The second square root is blamed on an unnamed "fault". The research gives the real cause: the root is set in both the transmitter and the controller, when it should be "either in the transmitter or in the controller (but not both)" (Control Engineering, notes 7.6). The brief promised this, and it would turn the screen into a warning from the real job.

The first order's 7 and 14 are fully visible only from the end of the 0.35 s screen fade until 0.45 s, then they fade out for the swap, so Dan barely sees the result he is meant to compare with 10. Hold them for about a second before the boxes move. The dimmed working line "g first: ... = 14" only partly makes up for this.

findings.what: The brief promised fg(x), the shorthand UK books use (Bitesize, notes 4.7), but no screen shows it. One cited line here ("UK books also write it fg(x), with g still first") would prepare him to read it.

"Lesson 8 shows why d is lesson 2's rule run backwards" is loose. Lesson 2's S(p) = 0.16p + 4 takes a percentage, so running it backwards gives 50 at 12 mA, not d's 0.5. Say "lesson 2's rule run backwards, giving a fraction instead of a percentage".
